extracted.intended_audience: regulated employers, small business stakeholders, regulatory analysts, and public commenters on OSHA's proposed heat injury and illness prevention standard
extracted.subtask_description: Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (IRFA) and related procedural/economic requirements for OSHA's proposed Heat Injury and Illness Prevention standard, including required IRFA elements, legal basis, small-entity impact estimation, and alternatives analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: IRFA required element: Description of reasons why action is being considered
rubrics_metrics.description: A description of the reasons why action by the agency is being considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must explain the public health/safety problem motivating the rule (e.g., heat is the leading cause of death among weather-related phenomena; heat-related illnesses and injuries statistics; underreporting concerns), prior agency activity (e.g., ANPRM), petitions, state regulations, stakeholder input, and other factual bases that justify rulemaking. OSHA cites BLS estimates, state standards, petitions (e.g., 2018 Public Citizen petition), and an ANPRM (86 FR 59309) as supporting background.

rubrics_metrics.name: IRFA required element: Succinct statement of objectives and legal basis
rubrics_metrics.description: A succinct statement of the objectives of, and legal basis for, the proposed rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Should state the rule's objective (here: reduce HRIs and fatalities by requiring HIIPPs, hazard identification/monitoring, rest breaks, water, training, emergency planning, etc.) and cite statutory authority (e.g., OSH Act of 1970, 29 U.S.C. 651 et seq.). Reference other sections (e.g., Pertinent Legal Authority) as needed to support legal basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: IRFA required element: Description and estimate of number of small entities affected
rubrics_metrics.description: A description of and, where feasible, an estimate of the number of small entities to which the proposed rule will apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use SBA/RFA definitions to characterize small entities and, where practicable, provide counts by industry/region/size class. OSHA provides detailed tabulations (e.g., estimate ~2.0 million small entities, ~16.2 million employees protected) and NAICS/region breakout tables. Include assumptions and data sources (BLS, Census, SBA, USDA, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: IRFA required element: Description of projected reporting, recordkeeping, and other compliance requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A description of the projected reporting, recordkeeping, and other compliance requirements of the proposed rule, including an estimate of the classes of small entities that will be subject to the requirements and the type of professional skills necessary for the preparation of the report or record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide detailed accounting of what compliance entails (e.g., HIIPP development, hazard identification, training, rest breaks, emergency planning), estimate per-establishment and per-employee one-time and annual costs, and specify any specialized skills or professional services required. OSHA describes its unit-cost methodology, frequency assumptions (e.g., indoor hazard evaluation every 5 years), and presents tables of one-time and annualized costs for small and very small entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: IRFA required element: Identification of relevant Federal rules that may duplicate/overlap/conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: An identification, to the extent practicable, of all relevant Federal rules which may duplicate, overlap, or conflict with the proposed rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe existing federal regulatory landscape and note potential duplication/overlap/conflict so commenters can assess harmonization or preemption issues. Provide citations and comparisons where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: IRFA required element: Description and discussion of significant alternatives to minimize economic impact
rubrics_metrics.description: A description and discussion of any significant alternatives to the proposed rule which accomplish the stated objectives of applicable statutes and which minimize any significant economic impact of the proposed rule on small entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss feasible alternatives such as (a) differing compliance or reporting requirements or timetables for small entities; (b) clarification, consolidation, or simplification of compliance and reporting requirements; (c) use of performance rather than design standards; and (d) exemptions from coverage. Evaluate how each alternative meets statutory objectives and its expected economic effects on affected small entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: RFA certification standard and screening test for small-entity impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 5 U.S.C. 605(b), the head of an agency may certify that the proposed rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities, but a factual basis must support such a certification; OSHA developed a screening test to consider minimum threshold effects on small entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The screening test is similar in concept to the revenue test used elsewhere (Section VIII.D.) and is applied specifically to small entities (SBA definitions). If OSHA cannot certify (i.e., screening indicates likely significant impacts), an IRFA is required. Provide factual/data support for any certification decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: OSH Act requirements for adopting a safety standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Before adopting a safety standard, OSHA must show the standard provides a high degree of employee protection, substantially reduces a significant risk, is technologically feasible, and is economically feasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite controlling precedent and guidance (e.g., 58 FR 16612; Int'l Union v. OSHA, 37 F.3d 665; Am. Iron & Steel Inst. v. OSHA, 939 F.2d 975). Explain each element and demonstrate how the proposed standard satisfies them in the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological feasibility (definition and test)
rubrics_metrics.description: A standard is technologically feasible if the protective measures it requires already exist, can be brought into existence with available technology, or can be created with technology that is reasonably expected to be developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide evidence that required protections are achievable with existing or reasonably foreseeable technology (cite Am. Iron and Steel Inst. v. OSHA). Consider industry practices, state standards, and expert input to support feasibility findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic feasibility (industry-level cost standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining economic feasibility, OSHA must consider the cost of compliance in an industry rather than on individual employers and must construct a reasonable estimate of compliance costs and demonstrate a reasonable likelihood that these costs will not threaten the existence or competitive structure of an industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use industry-level analyses (not firm-by-firm insolvency tests). Provide transparent cost-estimation methods, discuss uncertainties, and compare costs to industry revenues and competitive structure (citing case law). Address outliers where impacts may exceed thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology for estimating compliance costs for small and very small entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate costs by computing, for each 4-digit NAICS industry and State, the average one-time cost per establishment, average annual cost per establishment, average one-time cost per employee, and average annual cost per employee; multiply by counts of affected small establishments/employees and annualize one-time costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify assumptions (e.g., indoor hazard evaluation frequency every 5 years), data sources (BLS, Census, SBA), procedures for deriving per-establishment and per-employee costs, treatment of one-time vs periodic costs, and identical methodology for very small entities. Present detailed tables and sensitivity/uncertainty discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of costs-as-percentage-of-revenue metric (1% threshold) to assess significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare estimated annualized compliance costs to average annual revenue per entity to assess significance; OSHA reports impacts as a percentage of revenue and highlights industries where costs exceed one percent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report industry-by-industry percent impacts and flag those exceeding benchmarks (e.g., >1% of revenue) for further consideration; discuss potential over/underestimation sources (e.g., scheduling changes not modeled).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discount rate and annualization approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Annualize one-time costs using an explicit discount rate; OSHA uses a 2 percent discount rate for annualizing costs in these tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the discount rate used, rationale, and perform sensitivity analysis to alternative rates. Indicate how annualized totals incorporate potential labor-productivity cost savings (e.g., rest-break productivity effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of statutory or enforcement limitations affecting small-entity impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize statutory or appropriations constraints (e.g., Congressional budget rider limiting OSHA enforcement on small family-owned farms) that may affect whether particular small entities will incur enforcement or compliance costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify industries where enforcement limitations or other statutory constraints change the practical impact of the rule (e.g., small sheep/goat farms likely not subject to enforcement) and explain how that affects cost estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicitation of public comment on small-entity analysis assumptions and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA invites feedback on the analysis of impacts on small and very small entities and on choices such as including large non-profits in the small-entity profile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear opportunities for stakeholders to comment on methodology, data sources, assumptions (e.g., time spent outdoors), classification of entities, and alternative approaches; incorporate substantive comments into the final IRFA where appropriate.
